title: What is known about 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA0LF_0LC0RA_0RE---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA0LF_0LC0RA_0RE---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.

The run is a cascade of counters: at the left end a base-3 counter N with 3-cell digits (the wall of 101s of the first look is made of its top digits), at the right binary counters with 4-cell digits that obey the stream laws of the F02 two-word sweepers, and between them a middle part that is not decoded and grows about 15 cells per tenfold time. The laws of N and of the binary streams are proved in Lean for every size.
verdict: The question is open. No halt in 1011 steps of the C simulator; Lean proves no halt in the first 107 steps (native_decide) and the laws of the outer parts of the tape for every size.

Where a halt would come from. Only F1 halts and F is entered only from D reading 1 (0LF). That is rare: 82 times in 1011 steps, in three kinds of events (at the right end, a second series near it, and cascades that walk into N), always with a 0 left of D.
What is missing. The middle part between N and the binary counters: it is where the time goes and where the rare events start. Without its rules there is no macro-level accelerator and no invariant.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The halting pattern never forms
claims.text: F is entered only from D reading 1. That happens 72 times in the first 10<sup>8</sup> steps and 82 times in the first 10<sup>11</sup>, always with a 0 left of D, so F reads 0.

claims.title: The base-3 counter N, for every size
claims.text: Read the cells left of N's low end three at a time from the head outward, 010 = 0, 110 = 1, 100 = 2, blank beyond. A visit in state A adds one; it comes back out in B without carry and in E with a carry; a carry through all digits makes the blank into a new digit 2. Proved from five token rows by induction on the number of digits.

claims.title: The binary streams, for every size
claims.text: The stream laws of the F02 sibling 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB--- hold for this machine: in tokens z = 00, a = 10, c = 01, a visit in state B to an a/z stream is a binary increment, a visit in state A to the counter M (digits z c, c c) adds one and wraps, sending three visits into the stream after it.

claims.title: The run uses the counter law
claims.text: In the run, the cells left of -122 are entered only in state A, and all 426,172 of those visits, from step 588,436 to step 40,769,252, are rows of the counter law; then the middle reaches -122 and N's low end moves outward. At 10<sup>9</sup> steps N fills cells -191 to -143 (16 digits), at 10<sup>10</sup> about -206 to -158.

claims.title: Three parts of the tape
claims.text: The crossing profile at 10<sup>9</sup> steps (moves from each cell to the next): ×3 every 3 cells over -191 to -143 (N), no pattern over -143 to -60 (the middle), ×1/2 every 4 cells over -60 to -15 (binary counters with 4-cell digits), a few hundred over -15 to 47.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator runs 10<sup>11</sup> steps from blank tape without a halt; at the end cells -215 to 53 (269 cells), 116 ones; F entered 82 times in all. Cells visited: 164 (10<sup>6</sup>), 175 (10<sup>7</sup>), 222 (10<sup>8</sup>), 239 (10<sup>9</sup>), 258 (10<sup>10</sup>), 269 (10<sup>11</sup>).

claims.title: The middle grows and eats N
claims.text: Between 10<sup>9</sup> and 10<sup>10</sup> steps the left end moves from -191 to -206 and N's low end from -143 to about -158: N keeps about 16 digits and the middle grows about 15 cells per tenfold time. Its profile halves every 4 cells from -141 to -121 and has bumps at -115, -95, -77, -63, as if it held further binary counters. The 54 event rules of the F02 sibling hold for this table, but their event shape never occurs (none in 10<sup>8</sup> steps).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Needed: the rules of the middle part and of the rare D1 events, then whether D can ever read 1 with a 1 to its left.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same tapes at another pace, whatever the states, as 1 other holdout (listed on the explainer page).

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this machine runs a base-3 counter at its left end and binary counters at its right, both proved in Lean, with a middle part between them that nobody has decoded yet. This page runs the real machine in your browser and lists what is known.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 269 cells visited.
The base-3 counter and the binary streams, proved for every size.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
Where the time goes and the rare events start; not decoded.

sections.heading: Three parts of the tape
html: The run is a cascade of counters. At step 109 the tape (cells -191 to 47) splits into three parts, which show up plainly in the crossing profile, the number of times the head moves from each cell to the next one (c/cross.c):

cells at 109 stepscrossingspart
-191 to -143×3 every 3 cells (1, 11, 111, 1,003, 9,023, 81,209, … 19,736,834)N, a base-3 counter, 16 digits
-143 to -600.5 to 33 million, no simple patternthe middle, not decoded
-60 to -15×1/2 every 4 cells (791,259 at -55, 396,417 at -51 … 3,617 at -23)binary counters with 4-cell digits
-15 to 47a few hundred, falling to 1runs of 10 that grow by one word at rare right-end events

sections.heading: The left counter
html: The left counter N (proved). Read the cells left of N's low end three at a time, from the head outward: 010 = 0, 110 = 1, 100 = 2. Everything left of N is blank. A visit of the head in state A adds one: trailing 2s become 0s, the first other digit goes up by one, and the head comes back out in state B (no carry) or E (carry). A carry through every digit turns blank cells into a new digit 2. lean/Counter.lean proves this for every number of digits (n_inc0, n_inc1, n_inc0_carry, n_inc1_carry, n_overflow), from five token rows (lean/VisitL.lean, predicate VisL). The wall of 101s at the left end that the first description saw is made of N's top digits; its length wanders as N counts.

In the run, the cells left of -122 are entered only in state A, and every one of those 426,172 visits is one of these five rows, from the first at step 588,436 until step 40,769,252 (c/vislaws.c). After that the middle reaches -122: N's low end moves outward while digits are added at the top, so N stays at about 16 digits (cells -191 to -143 at 109, -206 to about -158 at 1010). The visited region grows mostly because the middle grows (about 15 cells per tenfold time), not because N does.

sections.heading: The binary streams on the right
html: The binary streams (proved). The right part uses the stream laws found for the sibling 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RA_0LB--- (family F02, two-word sweeper). In tokens of two cells (z = 00, a = 10, c = 01): a visit in state B to a stream of a's and z's turns the first z into a and every second a before it into z (a binary increment, vb_odd, vb_even, ve_odd), and a visit in state A to the counter M with digits z c = 0, c c = 1 adds one, with a wrap that sends three visits into the stream after it (m_inc, m_wrap). lean/Stream.lean proves them for this machine from 29 token rows mined at cell -40 (lean/VisitR.lean, proved with this machine's own table; it differs from the sibling's only in D1 and F0).

sections.heading: The rare events
html: The rare events. The only way into F (whose 1 halts) is D reading 1 (0LF). That happened 72 times in the first 108 steps, 74 by 109, 81 by 1010 and 82 by 1011 (c/longrun.c), always with a 0 to the left of D, so F reads 0. The events come in three kinds (c/d1ev.c): at the right end, after (10)^k (k grows by one each time), in a second series a few cells further left, and in cascades in which D appears every 3 cells going left (… [1] 0001011 …), the head walking into N. Whether a cascade can ever put a 1 left of D is the open question.

sections.heading: Relatives with the same engine
html: Machine family. Machines 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA0LF_0LC0RA_0RE---, 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA1LF_0LC0RE_0LA--- and 1RB0LD_0LC0RE_1LA0RD_0RB0LF_1RC1LA_0RB--- (mirrored, states renamed) all contain the engine of the F02 two-word sweepers (prefix 1RB0LE_1LC0RE_0RA0LD_1LA); all three satisfy the same counter law and the same stream laws. They differ only in D1, E1 and F0, which are used in the middle and at the rare events. The 54 event rules of the F02 sibling (its lean/Events.lean) also hold for this table (events.py of that folder proves all 54 for it; not added here), but the F02 event shape 0^inf 1 0 [N] A> 0 [M] 1 … never occurs in this run (none in 108 steps): here N and M are kept apart by the middle.

sections.heading: What is left
html:
• Decode the middle (cells -143 to -60 at 109): it grows by about 15 cells per tenfold time and eats N's low digits. Its crossing profile has steps of 4 cells (halving from -141 to -121) and bumps at -115, -95, -77 and -63, as if it held further binary counters fed by wraps.
  • Write the rare D1 events (the right-end series and the cascades into N) as rules on the counters.
  • Then: can D ever read 1 with a 1 to its left?

• Direct C simulation (c/longrun.c): 1011 steps, no halt; at the end cells -215 to 53 (269 cells), 116 ones. Cells visited: 164 (106), 175 (107), 222 (108), 239 (109), 258 (1010), 269 (1011).
  • No macro-level accelerator: the counter law and the stream laws describe the outer parts, but the time is spent in the middle, whose rules are not known, so no run beyond the direct one was possible.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 239 cells (191 left of the start, 47 right), with a density of 1s of 0.423.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same tapes at another pace (observed, not proved). Leave the states aside and compare only the tape and the place of the head. Then a large part of the first 107 configurations of this machine are configurations of the machines below, in the same order and up to the end of the run. The steps at which they occur differ, the tables are not renamings of each other, and equal tapes with different states may be continued differently, so this does not tie the halting questions together.

  • 1RB0LD_0LC0RE_1LA0RD_0RB0LF_1RC1LA_0RB--- (in a mirror): 9,285,736 configurations, the last at step 9,285,895 here and step 10,000,000 there

family: F02 engine with a different D1/F path: counters behind a growing middle
summary: A cascade of counters: a base-3 counter at the left end and binary counters at the right (both proved in Lean for every size), with an undecoded middle that grows about 15 cells per tenfold time.
